questions.prompt: One girl has a room of her own at home. How do you name that room?
questions.explanation: "the girl's room" is right: there is one owner, so the noun takes an apostrophe and an s, and the owner stands in front of what she owns. "the girls' room" puts the apostrophe after a plural and would need several girls. "the girls's room" adds an s to a plural that already has one, and "the room of the girl" copies a French construction English does not use for a person.

questions.prompt: Which part of a car does the driver use to see what is following her?
questions.explanation: "the rear-view mirror" is the one: rear means the back, so this mirror shows what is behind the car. "the steering wheel" is what she holds in her hands to choose her direction, "the headlights" are the lamps at the front that light the road ahead, and "the brake" is what she presses with her foot to slow down. Only one of the four turns her eyes towards the back of the car.

questions.prompt: In which of these sentences does what mean the thing that?

options.text: What about another cup of tea?

questions.explanation: "Is this what you wanted?" passes the test: say the thing that in its place and the sentence still works, since what stands for the object the person was hoping for. "What do you mean exactly?" opens a question and asks for a fact, "What about another cup of tea?" is the fixed frame of a suggestion, and "What a nice view!" is an exclamation that asks for nothing.

questions.prompt: The story runs from the visit at the centre to the last telephone call. Which tense carries those events?
questions.explanation: "the simple past" is the tense of narration: it lines up finished events one after the other, which is exactly what a story does. "the past progressive" would set a scene going on around them rather than move the story forward. "the present perfect" refuses a stated moment, and "the simple present" would turn the night into a routine that happens every evening.

questions.prompt: The voice on the telephone says: "Hurry up, I'm right behind you and if you keep driving this slowly we'll never get home." What do the words we'll never get home prove about the caller?

options.text: He is calling her from a public telephone box.
He is going to the same house as the narrator.
He wants the narrator to stop her car at once.
He has never met the narrator before that night.

questions.explanation: "He is going to the same house as the narrator." is what the words prove: we get home puts the two of them under one roof at the end of the journey. "He has never met the narrator before that night." is contradicted by that same we. "He is calling her from a public telephone box." cannot stand beside I'm right behind you, and "He wants the narrator to stop her car at once." reverses his message, since he is asking her to drive faster.
